processing: Fixed, rolled, shaped and dried, with hand versions tossed in very hot iron woks; industrial production also follows a set standard. The shaping leaves a downy, hook-curled leaf.
harvest_season: Spring. As with other Zhejiang greens, early picking is the prized part.
appearance_dry: Tight, downy, hook-curled strips of lustrous green, said to recall a monkey's paw.
taste_profile: Known for a lasting chestnut-like aroma and a brisk, mellow, full-flavoured mouth.

brewing.notes: Typical for a downy curled green. Water just off a strong simmer brings out the chestnut note; long steeps turn it sharp.

vintage_note: Sold as the current-year spring green, usually graded by tenderness and date, and best within the year. Songyang is home to a major green tea market, so the name also appears on a lot of ordinary tea. Look for the protected-origin mark and a harvest date.
description:
Songyang Yinhou, silver monkey, is the flagship green tea of Songyang county in Lishui, southwest Zhejiang. The name comes from the leaf: silver down over a curled, hooked strip said to look like a monkey's paw.

The tea gets its hook through rolling and shaping, including in very hot iron woks when made by hand. Machine production follows a set standard too, so not every bag has seen the traditional process.

Local promotion sums up its qualities as green colour, tight strips, high aroma and strong flavour, and writers single out a lasting chestnut scent. Brew it a bit warmer than a pure bud tea, but watch the time.

The county is known for the South Zhejiang tea market, one of China's main green tea hubs. Good Yinhou sits next to plenty of cheap tea there, so even hooks, visible down and a clear date are what to check.

Do not mix it up with Bai Mao Hou from Fujian, or with other teas that have monkey in the name, which are quite different.
history:
Tea growing in Songyang is said to go back to the Three Kingdoms, with tribute status claimed for the Tang; those claims are local. Better grounded is the first-class award reported for Songyang tea at the 1929 West Lake Exposition, which went to the county's tea and not to this particular product.

Yinhou itself is modern. One account has the county agriculture bureau creating the downy, hooked form in 1981, building on older methods and local plants, with the title of Zhejiang famous tea following in 1984 and national geographical indication protection in 2008.
